note: Trait ontology of the swarm genome. A trait is a behavioural or structural property of a collective that a coder can mark present or absent from published evidence. Each trait names the flags (research/FLAGS.md) and P1 primitives it maps to, so the matrix can be compiled into a regime.

axes.name: Signalling
axes.question: How does information pass between members?

axes.name: Field and memory
axes.question: What persists outside a single member?

axes.name: Activation and recruitment
axes.question: What makes members start or stop working on something?

axes.name: Collective decision
axes.question: How does the group commit to one option?

axes.name: Division of labour and structure
axes.question: Who does what, and is anyone in charge?

axes.name: Regulation and termination
axes.question: How does the group hold a set point, share load and end an effort?

axes.name: Defence and integrity
axes.question: How does the group recognise, contain and repair what harms it?

traits.name: Contact signalling
traits.definition: Information passes by direct physical contact or very short range encounter between two members (antennation, trophallaxis, cell-cell contact signalling).

traits.name: Broadcast chemical signal
traits.definition: Members release a diffusible chemical that many others sense at once (pheromone plume, autoinducer, cAMP wave).

traits.name: Quality-graded recruitment signal
traits.definition: The strength, duration or rate of a recruitment signal scales with the quality of the resource or option found (waggle-dance circuits, trail strength by food quality).

traits.name: Alarm signal
traits.definition: A dedicated signal announces danger and changes the behaviour of members who did not see the threat (alarm pheromone, alarm call, danger signal).

traits.name: Inhibitory or stop signal
traits.definition: A signal whose effect is to stop, suppress or redirect the activity of others (stop signal, negative pheromone, inhibitory cue).

traits.name: Local neighbour coupling
traits.definition: Each member aligns or responds to a small set of nearby members (metric or topological neighbours) rather than to the whole group, and group order arises from these local interactions.

traits.name: Stigmergic deposit
traits.definition: Members modify a shared environment (trail, structure, substrate, matrix) and the modification cues the later behaviour of others.

traits.name: Signal decay
traits.definition: Deposited cues fade with time unless renewed (pheromone evaporation, signal degradation, tube retraction without flow).

traits.name: Persistent shared structure
traits.definition: The group builds or keeps a durable structure that stores the outcome of past work and is used by later members (nest, comb, mound, biofilm matrix, tube network).

traits.name: Individual learning and memory
traits.definition: Individual members learn and retain information (routes, locations, partners) that changes their own later behaviour in the collective task.

traits.name: Response-threshold variation
traits.definition: Members differ in the stimulus level at which they take up a task, so the number engaged rises with the stimulus.

traits.name: Density-triggered collective switch
traits.definition: Above a density or signal concentration the group switches to a qualitatively different collective behaviour (quorum sensing gene expression, solitarious-to-gregarious phase, aggregation).

traits.name: Positive-feedback recruitment
traits.definition: Engaged members recruit others, so engagement amplifies itself (mass recruitment, relay of a recruitment signal).

traits.name: Inactive reserve
traits.definition: A sizeable fraction of members is idle most of the time and is engaged when demand rises or workers are lost.

traits.name: Self-limiting recruitment
traits.definition: Recruitment carries its own brake: a negative feedback that ends or caps the recruitment wave without an outside regulator.

traits.name: Minimum group size for payoff
traits.definition: The collective task yields nothing below a minimum number of participants and pays only above it (cooperative predation, cooperative digestion, group hunting of large prey).

traits.name: Quorum decision
traits.definition: The group commits when the number of members supporting an option passes a threshold, not when all agree.

traits.name: Cross-inhibition between options
traits.definition: Supporters of one option actively suppress support for a competing option, breaking deadlock.

traits.name: Independent parallel exploration
traits.definition: Several members explore alternatives independently before the group commits (scouts, independent searchers).

traits.name: Informed-minority guidance
traits.definition: A few members holding information (experience, knowledge of a target) steer the movement or choice of the group without being recognised leaders.

traits.name: Tunable speed-accuracy trade-off
traits.definition: The group changes how fast it decides depending on urgency or option quality, trading accuracy for speed (quorum lowered under harsh conditions).

traits.name: Morphological castes
traits.definition: Members differ in body form or cell type in ways tied to the tasks they perform (soldiers, majors and minors, spore and stalk cells).

traits.name: Temporal polyethism
traits.definition: Members change tasks with age or developmental stage in a regular sequence.

traits.name: Reproductive division
traits.definition: Only some members reproduce; the others work (queen and workers, germ and soma, breeding pair).

traits.name: Persistent leader or dominance hierarchy
traits.definition: A stable individual or rank order directs group movement, access or task assignment. Presence of this trait means the collective is not leaderless.

traits.name: Task partitioning with handoff
traits.definition: A task is split into sequential stages done by different members, with material or information handed over between them.

traits.name: Self-assembled bodies
traits.definition: Members link their own bodies into a functional structure (bridge, raft, bivouac, chain, fruiting body, slug).

traits.name: Collective homeostasis
traits.definition: The group regulates a shared variable around a set point by negative feedback (nest temperature, colony size, oxygen, osmotic balance).

traits.name: Active termination
traits.definition: The group ends a collective effort by an active process, not only by members drifting away (resolution of inflammation, swarm dispersal signal, contraction after expansion).

traits.name: Rotation of costly positions
traits.definition: Members take turns in a position that is costly or exposed (leading a formation, outer edge of a huddle).

traits.name: Synchronisation
traits.definition: Members align the timing of an action without a pacemaker (synchronous flashing, synchronised emergence, oscillations).

traits.name: Elastic group size
traits.definition: The number of active members grows and shrinks with demand within one bout (fission-fusion, clonal expansion and contraction, recruitment and retirement of foragers).

traits.name: Member recognition
traits.definition: Members discriminate group members from non-members (nestmate recognition, kin recognition, self and non-self recognition).

traits.name: Cheater control
traits.definition: The group limits members that take the benefit of cooperation without paying its cost (policing, sanctions, exclusion of non-producers).

traits.name: Social immunity and quarantine
traits.definition: The group detects infected or compromised members or material and isolates, cleans or removes them (hygienic behaviour, allogrooming, sick-member exclusion, removal of corpses).

traits.name: Scaled collective defence
traits.definition: The defensive response grows with the size of the threat by recruiting more defenders (mobbing, mass stinging, swarming on an intruder).

traits.name: Sacrificial defence
traits.definition: Members defend the group at a lethal or reproductive cost to themselves (autothysis, barbed sting, suicidal guards, altruistic cell death).

traits.name: Structural repair and redundancy
traits.definition: The group repairs damage to its structure or keeps redundant members so the function survives losses (rebuilding, regrowing network links, replacing lost workers).

traits.name: Sentinel or vigilance sharing
traits.definition: Some members watch for danger while others work, and the watch is shared or rotated.

conditions.name: Typical group size
conditions.definition: log10 of the typical number of members in one functioning collective.

conditions.name: Relatedness
conditions.definition: Genetic relatedness among members of a typical group.

conditions.name: Group permanence
conditions.definition: Whether the collective persists across the life of members, forms seasonally, or forms for one bout.

conditions.name: Spatial structure
conditions.definition: Central nest or site, moving group, attached to a substrate, or a fluid aggregate with no fixed site.

conditions.name: Main collective problems
conditions.definition: The problems the collective behaviour mainly solves.

conditions.name: Parasite and predator pressure
conditions.definition: Pressure from parasites, pathogens, predators or social cheaters on the group.

conditions.name: Environmental change
conditions.definition: How fast the resources or conditions the group depends on change relative to a bout of collective work.

conditions.name: Information access
conditions.definition: Whether a member normally sees only its neighbourhood or the state of the whole group.

conditions.name: Individual cognitive capacity
conditions.definition: Capacity of a single member to learn and plan (cells minimal, insects low, fish and birds medium, social mammals high).
